title: Two Promised Sons: John and Jesus Announced
summary: Luke opens with a formal preface explaining that he has investigated everything carefully to write an orderly account for Theophilus. In the temple the angel Gabriel tells the aged priest Zechariah that his barren wife Elizabeth will bear a son, John, who will prepare the way for the Lord; Zechariah doubts and is struck mute. Six months later Gabriel tells Mary, a virgin in Nazareth, that she will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear Jesus, the Son of God and heir of David's throne. Mary visits Elizabeth and sings of God's mercy, John is born and named, and Zechariah, his speech restored, prophesies God's salvation.
story: The Old Testament closed with a promise that God would send his messenger, Elijah, before the day of the Lord (Malachi 3:1, 4:5-6), and in the traditional reckoning of both Jews and Christians no new prophetic voice arose for about four centuries after it. Luke begins the story again in the temple, among faithful Jews who have been waiting, and he tells it in language that sounds like the Old Testament on purpose. Zechariah and Elizabeth are Abraham and Sarah again, and Mary's song echoes Hannah's. The chapter sets up the whole Gospel: two births announced, two sons whose roles are distinct, John the forerunner and Jesus the Lord, and a God who is keeping the promises he made to Abraham and David. Everything that follows in Luke and Acts flows from what God begins here.
historical:
Herod, called king of Judea in verse 5, is Herod the Great, who ruled Judea for Rome from 37 BC until his death in 4 BC. He was a gifted and ruthless ruler, a great builder who began rebuilding the Jerusalem temple on a lavish scale around 20 BC, and a man feared even by his own family. The events of this chapter therefore take place in the last years of his reign, shortly before 4 BC.

The temple was served by priests descended from Aaron, divided into twenty-four divisions that took turns serving for a week at a time, twice a year, and at the great festivals. The division of Abijah was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10). With thousands of priests, duties were assigned by lot, and according to later Jewish tradition a priest could be chosen to burn the incense in the holy place only once in his lifetime. The incense was offered morning and evening, while worshipers prayed in the courts outside. Zechariah's moment in the sanctuary was likely the high point of his priestly life. Nazareth, by contrast, was a small and obscure village in Galilee, unmentioned in the Old Testament, which makes the contrast between the two announcements pointed: one in the holy place in Jerusalem, one in a village no one expected anything from.
cultural:
Barrenness in the ancient world was a deep grief and often a public shame, which is why Elizabeth speaks of God taking away her disgrace (verse 25). It was usually blamed on the woman. The Old Testament tells several stories of barren women whom God opened to bear children of destiny: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson's mother, and Hannah. Luke's readers who knew their Scriptures would recognize the pattern at once. John's abstention from wine and strong drink resembles the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, and like Samson and Samuel he is set apart from birth.

Marriage in first-century Judaism took place in two stages. Betrothal, the pledge, was a binding legal agreement, made while girls were often still young, commonly in their teens; it could be ended only by divorce. Some months later the bride moved into her husband's home and the marriage was completed. Mary was betrothed to Joseph but not yet living with him. Naming a son on the day of his circumcision, the eighth day as commanded in Genesis 17:12, was customary, and sons were usually named after a father or relative, which is why the neighbors object to the name John. Zechariah writes on a tablet, a wooden board coated with wax.
literary: Luke's preface (verses 1 to 4) is a single long sentence in polished literary Greek, in the style of Greek historians, naming his sources and purpose. Then, from verse 5, his Greek changes and begins to sound like the Greek Old Testament, as if the story itself required the language of Scripture. The chapter is built on parallels between John and Jesus: two announcements by Gabriel, two questions in response (Zechariah's doubting question and Mary's wondering one), two births, and two songs. Each time, Jesus is shown to be greater. The two strands meet when the two pregnant women greet each other and the unborn John leaps. The chapter includes two of the church's oldest hymns, Mary's song (verses 46 to 55, traditionally called the Magnificat from its first word in Latin) and Zechariah's (verses 68 to 79, called the Benedictus). Both are woven almost entirely from Old Testament phrases.

outline.t: Gabriel announces John's birth to Zechariah
Gabriel announces Jesus' birth to Mary
The birth and naming of John

doctrines.note: Gabriel's words gather Israel's royal hopes onto Jesus: he will be called Son of the Most High, receive the throne of his father David, and reign over the house of Jacob with a kingdom that will never end, the promise first made to David in 2 Samuel 7:12-16. Zechariah praises God for raising up a horn of salvation in David's house.

The Holy Spirit is active throughout: John will be filled with the Spirit from the womb, the Spirit will come upon Mary so that her child will be called holy, and Elizabeth and Zechariah are filled with the Spirit and speak. The church confesses on this chapter's witness that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary.

Mary and Zechariah both interpret these births as God remembering his covenant, the oath he swore to Abraham, and his promises through the prophets. What happens here is not a new idea but God keeping his word, which Gabriel sums up in verse 37: no word from God will ever fail.

Zechariah, a righteous priest, asks for proof and is silenced; Mary, a young woman in a village, asks how and then surrenders: I am the Lord's servant. Elizabeth names the difference: blessed is she who has believed. Faith is trust in God's word before its fulfillment is seen.

words.note: Charitoo, to favor or bestow grace. Gabriel greets Mary as one who has been favored, a perfect passive participle meaning she has been graced by God. The emphasis falls on God's free choice, not on Mary's merit, and verse 30 restates it: you have found favor with God. The same verb describes believers in Ephesians 1:6, blessed in the Beloved.

Episkiazo, to overshadow. In the Greek Old Testament it describes the cloud of God's glory settling on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35), and Luke uses it again of the cloud at the transfiguration (9:34). Gabriel's words present the conception of Jesus as an act of God's creative presence, not a divine union of the kind found in pagan myths.

Tapeinosis, lowliness or humiliation. Mary sings that God has looked on the humble state of his servant, and Hannah used the same word in the Greek Old Testament when she prayed for a son (1 Samuel 1:11). The word introduces a theme of the whole Gospel: God lifts up the lowly and brings down the proud.

Anatole, a rising, especially of the sun, hence the east and the dawn. Zechariah speaks of the Dawn that will visit us from on high. In the Greek Old Testament the same word translates the Hebrew for Branch, a title for the coming king from David's line (Jeremiah 23:5, Zechariah 3:8, 6:12), so both images may be in play: a sunrise and a royal shoot.

christ: Luke 1 says more about who Jesus is before his birth than any other chapter in the Gospels. He is Jesus, whose name means the Lord saves. He is the Son of the Most High and the Son of God, conceived by the Holy Spirit. He is the heir of David who will reign forever, fulfilling 2 Samuel 7 and the prophets. Elizabeth calls him my Lord while he is still unborn, and John leaps for joy in his presence. Zechariah's song calls his coming a visit from God himself, the Dawn from on high shining on those in darkness, echoing Isaiah 9:2. The chapter also shows the character of his coming: he comes through a humble young woman in an obscure village, and God's mercy scatters the proud and lifts the humble, a pattern his whole life will follow.

hard.q: Is the virginal conception of Jesus history or legend?
hard.a: The church has confessed from its earliest creeds that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. Some modern scholars doubt it, noting that Mark, John, and Paul do not mention it, and that ancient literature contains stories of heroes and rulers with divine fathers. Those who defend the historical reading answer that Matthew and Luke tell the story independently, from different angles (Joseph's in Matthew, Mary's in Luke), which suggests an older tradition behind both; that the silence of other writers is not denial, since they begin their accounts later or write letters on other topics; and that the pagan parallels involve gods physically uniting with women, which is quite unlike Luke's reverent account of the Spirit's overshadowing with no hint of a divine partner. Some have also argued that early rumors of Jesus' illegitimacy, which appear to be reflected in later Jewish polemic, show that the unusual circumstances of his birth were known. Luke himself presents the account as part of what he carefully investigated. For historic Christianity this is part of the confession of who Jesus is: fully human, born of a woman, and fully God, the Son whose life did not begin in Mary's womb but was entered there.

questions: Zechariah and Elizabeth were faithful for decades while their deepest prayer went unanswered. How does their story speak to prayers you have been praying for a long time?
Mary asked a real question and then said, “I am the Lord's servant.” What would it look like for you to bring your honest questions to God and still say yes?
Mary sings that God brings down rulers and exalts the humble. Where do you see that pattern in Scripture, and where might it challenge your own position?
